::: {.hidden}
$$
\newcommand{\expr}[3]{\begin{array}{c}
#1 \\
\bbox[lightblue,5px]{#2}
\end{array} ⊢ #3}
\newcommand{\ct}[1]{\bbox[font-size: 0.8em]{\mathsf{#1}}}
\newcommand{\abbr}[1]{\bbox[transform: scale(0.95)]{\mathtt{#1}}}
\def\true{\ct{T}}
\def\false{\ct{F}}
$$
:::

In [Syntactic categories](../applicative_cg/syn_types.html), we said that intransitive verbs have the syntactic category $(np\backslash s)$:
they take a noun phrase to their left, and together with it, they produce a sentence.
And because they have this category, they have the semantic type $(e → t)$:
they take an entity as their semantic argument, and they produce a truth value---that is, they are interpreted as characteristic functions.

Take the verb *slept* as an example.

(@ex-slept) Frodo slept.

To derive the sentence in (@ex-slept), we can assign *Frodo* and *slept* the lexical entries in (@ex-lexicon).

(@ex-lexicon) $⟨\textit{Frodo}, \ct{f}⟩ ⊢ np$ <br>
	$⟨\textit{slept}, (λx.\ct{sleep}(x))⟩ ⊢ (np\backslash s)$

As usual, $\ct{f}$ is an entity---some element of the domain of whatever model we happen to be considering:
$$\ct{f} ∈ D_{e}$$
Meanwhile, $(λx.\ct{sleep}(x))$ is a characteristic function of a set of elements of this very same domain:
$$(λx.\ct{sleep}(x)) : (e → t)$$
It takes an entity, and it gives you back a truth value ($\true$ or $\false$).

Note the notation being used here:
'$(λx.\ct{sleep}(x))$'.
This is known as *λ-notation*.
It allows one to write functions down *anonymously*---i.e., without giving them names like $g_{\textit{slept}}$.
By using this notation, we are able to describe any given function's behavior simply in the way that we notate it.
In the case of $(λx.\ct{sleep}(x))$, we are saying that the function first takes an argument ($x$) and returns a truth value---either $\true$ or $\false$, depending on whether or not $x$ slept.

Exactly which characteristic function is $\ct{sleep}$?
We are not actually specifying this one way or the other.
Instead, we are using the expression '$\ct{sleep}$' to stand for $I_{\mathcal{M}}(\textit{slept})$, for whatever the model $\mathcal{M}$ happens to be.

Using the lexical entries for *Frodo* and *slept*, we can derive the sentence in (@ex-slept):

$$\begin{prooftree}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo}, \ct{f}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{slept}, (λx.\ct{sleep}(x))⟩ ⊢ (np\backslash s)\)}
\RightLabel{\(\backslash\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo slept}, (λx.\ct{sleep}(x))(\ct{f})⟩ ⊢ s\)}
\end{prooftree}$$
As we'd expect, given the semantic type of $s$ (i.e., $t$), the meaning derived for the entire sentence,

$$(λx.\ct{sleep}(x))(\ct{f})$$

is a truth value---$\true$ or $\false$, depending on which of these values $\ct{sleep}$ maps $\ct{f}$ to.
To see what this meaning is more clearly, we can use β-reduction to substitute the argument $\ct{f}$ in for the variable $x$ inside the function:

$$(λx.\ct{sleep}(x))(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ \ct{sleep}(\ct{f})$$
